items.streamTitle: Acute anxiety reduced task engagement less consistently among people with higher trait anxiety
items.streamSummary: Two online experiments involving 107 and 572 participants tested how current anxiety, typical anxiety levels, and task difficulty jointly relate to engagement. Contrary to the authors’ main hypothesis, higher state anxiety predicted less engagement primarily among low-trait-anxiety participants, with the task-difficulty pattern changing between experiments. The study offers evidence against a simple claim that anxiety always increases effort avoidance. Findings partly replicated, but engagement measures and the inconsistent difficulty interaction limit how precisely the effect can be generalized.

items.streamTitle: Only one of 18 low-resource radiation-oncology studies showed multi-stage AI integration
items.streamSummary: A systematic review of 18 studies from low- and middle-income settings assessed how far radiation-oncology AI has progressed from isolated model tasks to sustained clinical operation. Nine studies were task-level demonstrations, six showed clinician-supervised workflow integration, and only one described coordination across workflow stages. None met the review’s highest operational category, and continuous performance monitoring was not reported. This is a deployment-maturity assessment rather than proof that the systems are ineffective. It highlights infrastructure, validation, personnel and governance as barriers between successful prototypes and reliable clinical services.
items.attribution: Ndassi et al. — npj Digital Medicine

items.streamTitle: Hierarchical position and driving influence disagreed in a participatory workforce model
items.streamSummary: Researchers mapped 21 proposed causes of graduate job mismatch in Malaysia using Total Interpretive Structural Modeling and MICMAC analysis. The results showed why model interpretation matters: labor-market conditions and socioeconomic background were classified as drivers, while gender shared their hierarchical level but was not classified the same way. Personal interests also had high driving power despite a different level. The study provides an organized map of expert and literature-derived judgments, not observational identification of causal effects. It is especially useful for avoiding mistaken interpretations of network hierarchy as intervention priority.
items.attribution: Sahran, Ashaari & Ali Othman — Humanities and Social Sciences Communications

items.streamTitle: Forest walks produced more positive ratings and a matching facial-muscle signal
items.streamSummary: Researchers used wearable facial electromyography while people walked forest and city routes, then collected moment-by-moment emotional ratings with the aid of first-person video. Forest walking was associated with more positive reported feelings and reduced corrugator-muscle activity, a signal consistent with more positive emotional valence. The correspondence strengthens measurement beyond self-report alone, but it does not isolate trees or greenery as the causal ingredient, nor does it show lasting psychological benefit. The study is a useful example of matching physiological measurement to emotional valence rather than arousal alone.

items.streamTitle: Anthropic launched critical-infrastructure and open-source cyber programs, but remediation remains the test
items.streamSummary: Anthropic announced a Cyber Mission that pairs frontier AI models and on-site engineers with critical-infrastructure security providers, while offering free recurring AI vulnerability scans to participating open-source projects. The initiative targets electricity, water, transport, government systems, and shared software. It is a real program launch, not evidence that incident rates have fallen. Anthropic itself emphasizes that identifying flaws can be easier than verifying and safely fixing them, particularly in industrial environments that cannot be taken offline casually. The next meaningful outcomes are validated repairs, false-report burden, and reduced operational risk.

items.streamTitle: Six-country review found health-AI assessment rules poorly address generative systems that change over time
items.streamSummary: A comparison of 56 health-technology assessment documents across six countries found that randomized trials and cost-effectiveness studies remain central, with growing acceptance of real-world evidence. Yet current guidance often lacks specific methods for evaluating generative AI whose responses vary between runs or whose behavior changes after updates. The study is a policy-analysis review rather than a test of regulatory effectiveness. Its practical implication is that validation should cover model versions, stochastic variability, real-world performance, equity, and continuous monitoring—not just a one-time average accuracy estimate.
items.attribution: van Kessel et al. — npj Digital Medicine

items.streamTitle: NATO reported 300 uncrewed systems at REPMUS and advanced its Arctic mission-network trials
items.streamSummary: NATO’s October 8 account of REPMUS 2026 says the Portuguese-led maritime exercise involved more than 3,700 participants, 300 uncrewed systems, 60 research companies, and 36 navies. The new detail is the Task Force X-Arctic work on a common mission-engineering layer and connectivity backbone, ahead of another trial planned in Norway. Earlier accounts emphasized individual anti-submarine demonstrations; this release shows the larger integration architecture. Participation and testing do not establish effective detection or resilient operation under adversarial conditions, for which public comparative metrics remain unavailable.

items.streamTitle: A new open-source method separates behavioral contagion from coincidental timing
items.streamSummary: SPREAD is an open-source R framework that compares observed event timing with shuffled baselines while accounting for how often each individual acts. Researchers demonstrated it using more than 1,000 laughter events and 1,400 eating events in three-person groups. Laughter and eating showed different response-time patterns, illustrating why a single fixed time window can mislead. The method quantifies temporal clustering rather than proving person-to-person causation; its pointwise tests and timestamp permutations also require attention to multiple comparisons and within-person temporal dependence.

items.streamTitle: NATO scheduled its annual nuclear-readiness exercise with 17 nations and no live weapons
items.streamSummary: NATO announced that Steadfast Noon will begin October 13 in Italy with 17 participating countries. The recurring exercise tests procedures supporting the Alliance’s nuclear deterrence posture and does not involve live nuclear weapons. NATO says it is planned in advance, unrelated to any particular current event, and not directed against a specific country. The announcement is evidence of a readiness and signaling activity, not proof of improved deterrence or a measured change in Russian behavior. It illustrates why operational exercises, declared messages, external interpretations, and strategic effects must be evaluated separately.

items.streamTitle: Everyday drinking tracked alcohol cues and social context more consistently than negative mood
items.streamSummary: Two smartphone-sampling cohorts—73 adults with alcohol use disorder and 56 young adults with risky drinking—found that exposure to alcohol cues tracked momentary drinking even after adjusting for companionship, affect, arousal, and event appraisal. Companions and energetic arousal also showed reproducible associations, whereas negative mood did not. Exploratory individual-level analyses suggested different cue-reactive and socially reactive profiles. Because exposure and drinking were observed rather than randomized, the findings identify useful real-world correlates and candidate profiles, not proven intervention mechanisms.

items.streamTitle: Survey respondents wanted roughly 90% sensitivity and specificity from AI disease screening
items.streamSummary: A nationwide survey of 1,222 people plus 106 long-term lung-cancer survivors asked how many missed diagnoses and false alarms they would tolerate from AI-based disease detection. Average minimum acceptable sensitivity and specificity were both near 90%, with respondents who had cancer histories generally demanding stronger performance. These are expressed preferences, not proof that people would reject a particular device or that 90% is clinically sufficient. Screening decisions still depend on disease prevalence, severity, treatment consequences, and the balance between missed cases and unnecessary follow-up.
items.attribution: Yu et al. — npj Digital Medicine

items.streamTitle: Simple synthetic-data generators often matched or beat deep models in 2,220 benchmark runs
items.streamSummary: A preregistered benchmark compared simple statistical generators, SMOTE variants, and deep tabular generators over 2,220 runs, including small clinical datasets. Deep methods almost never beat the best simple baseline by more than random-seed noise; the simple baseline won 40 of 49 dataset-size conditions. The authors’ prediction of especially unstable rankings at small samples was not supported. Most top-two method differences were themselves smaller than seed variation. The result is preprint evidence, but it makes a strong case for evaluating synthetic data on actual downstream utility rather than algorithmic sophistication.

items.streamTitle: Training coding agents to verify their own fixes improved repair success and reduced false acceptance
items.streamSummary: A preprint on autonomous software-repair agents found that repeated attempts often searched the same locations and self-written tests accepted incorrect patches. The researchers trained agents to diversify edits and verify fixes against stronger labeled counterexamples. On 270 held-out issues, single-attempt resolution rose from 31.9% to 43.0%, eight-attempt success reached 60.7%, and verifier precision improved from 26.8% to 41.7%. These are benchmark results with uneven transfer across test suites, but they show why verification quality should be measured separately from the number of generated fixes.

items.streamTitle: Dutch software linked multiple drone sensors and interceptors into one air-defense workflow
items.streamSummary: In a Dutch airbase trial observed by Reuters, Intelic’s Nexus software brought radar detections, camera and reconnaissance-drone verification, and an AI-guided interceptor into one command interface. A human made the final launch decision. The firm has a €30 million Dutch defense contract and says the system is being deployed in Ukraine to connect equipment from different suppliers. The trial demonstrates workflow integration rather than combat effectiveness: public figures for false identification, engagement success, latency savings, and degraded-network performance are absent. Those measures will determine the practical value of the system.

items.streamTitle: A drone strike halted a major Yandex data center while core services reportedly remained online
items.streamSummary: Yandex said a drone strike on its Sasovo data center caused a fire and suspended operations at the facility, which houses tens of thousands of servers. Affected cloud customers were directed toward other zones, while the company reported that core consumer services remained available. The extent of hardware damage and any effect on the site’s AI supercomputing resources were not disclosed. The strike extends wartime infrastructure risk to a major Russian data hub and illustrates why redundancy, service continuity, recovery time, and physical damage must be assessed separately.

items.streamTitle: Detailed infographics and AI-rewritten text performed poorly for students screening positive for ADHD symptoms
items.streamSummary: A controlled study of 70 university students compared eight ways of presenting information, including text, charts, infographics, and AI-modified wording. Thirty students screened positive for ADHD symptoms. The best-performing formats were relatively simple, while detailed infographics and AI-modified text were associated with substantially poorer performance in the positive-screen group. Reported preferences sometimes diverged from measured speed and accuracy. The sample was small, and a positive screening result is not an ADHD diagnosis, but the study shows why digital accessibility should be tested behaviorally rather than inferred from appearance or user preference alone.

items.streamTitle: A review found only one completed prospective study of AI decision support during surgery
items.streamSummary: A scoping review screened 3,020 records on AI decision support used during surgery and found only five eligible prospective efforts. Just one had published clinical feasibility results, based on five patients; the other four were registered or ongoing studies without reported outcomes. None described comprehensive decision logging, model-update procedures, or subgroup-performance analysis. The authors proposed a conceptual ethics and implementation scorecard, but did not validate it as a regulatory tool. The review underscores how quickly technical systems can advance ahead of prospective effectiveness, human-oversight, and auditability evidence.
items.attribution: Parikh et al. — npj Digital Surgery

items.streamTitle: Danish intelligence says sabotage against Ukraine-linked defense production has intensified
items.streamSummary: Denmark’s domestic intelligence service says sabotage operations are increasingly targeting companies that supply Ukraine rather than aiming only at broad disruption. An official described the recruitment of low-level proxies through social platforms, sometimes beginning with simple reconnaissance before escalating. The service assesses that earlier tactics failed to deter NATO support and that weapons production is now a higher priority. Russia denies the accusations. This is an intelligence assessment, not an independently demonstrated account of Moscow’s intent or sabotage effectiveness, but it raises concrete concerns about defense-industrial security and proxy recruitment.

items.streamTitle: Personality-relevant movie scenes revealed more diverse brain responses among people high in neuroticism
items.streamSummary: An fMRI study of 174 people watching movies found that higher neuroticism was associated with more variable brain responses across individuals, particularly during scenes independently rated as relevant to the trait. Rather than identifying one uniform neural signature of neuroticism, the study found greater heterogeneity. The work supports the view that personality expression depends partly on situational context, but these are correlational group-level analyses. They do not explain the mechanism, establish clinical prediction, or justify inferring an individual’s personality from one brain scan.

items.streamTitle: An OpenAlex knowledge graph mapped 189,581 battery papers into searchable research expertise
items.streamSummary: A new paper demonstrates a cross-institutional research knowledge graph built from 189,581 battery-related publications in OpenAlex. The system combines broad bibliographic concepts with fine-grained keyphrases, weights topics by publication recency and authorship, and exposes researcher similarities through an RDF/Wikidata-linked interface. It offers a reusable architecture for finding expertise and adjacent topics without depending exclusively on coauthorship. However, about 30% of publications lacked abstracts, and inherited author-identity errors can distort similarity. The current demonstration supports discovery, not reliable prediction of future collaborations.

items.streamTitle: Technology-supported learning improved reported metacognition, but most evidence was self-report
items.streamSummary: A three-level meta-analysis of 33 studies found higher reported metacognitive outcomes following technology-supported learning interventions (Hedges’ g = 0.653). However, results varied considerably, technology type did not explain the differences, and exploratory advantages for immediate feedback or instructional guidance were not significant after multiple-testing correction. Most important, 90 of 94 effect sizes came from self-report measures. The evidence supports a promising educational role for technology, but does not establish equivalent improvements in actual monitoring, strategy use, or independent learning.

items.streamTitle: Agent setup mattered more than model size in a scientific workflow benchmark
items.streamSummary: An arXiv benchmark varied instructions, information, verification, time limits, and model backbone across four scientific coding-agent tasks and released more than 18,000 trajectories. Roughly 54% of measured outcome variance came from repeating the same configuration, and the information supplied to agents mattered more than model size or time budget. Asking agents to verify had little effect, whereas giving them a dedicated verification tool altered their behavior. The evidence is limited to these tasks, but it reinforces that reliable agents are engineered systems, not just language models.

items.streamTitle: Communication changed the pattern of crowd decisions without shortening the time to reach them
items.streamSummary: An experiment with 444 people in small and larger anonymous crowds tested movement decisions under uncertainty, with or without verbal communication. Communication did not significantly shorten the time to reach a final arrangement. It could be associated with either strong agreement or polarization, while fully uniform outcomes were uncommon without speech. The intended shared-identity manipulation did not work, and there were too few group runs to support strong conclusions about all decision distributions. The study is useful because it challenges the idea that communication simply accelerates crowd consensus.

items.streamTitle: Tesla's European FSD safety evidence did not support its strongest life-saving claims, outside researchers told Reuters
items.streamSummary: A Reuters investigation reviewed Tesla's European FSD safety studies, regulatory correspondence, and assessments from seven traffic-safety researchers. Because the company had too few European FSD miles for a meaningful crash-rate comparison, it relied on surrogate behaviors such as hard braking, horn use, turn signals, acceleration, and cornering. Researchers said several proxies were weak and the evidence did not show that FSD prevents fatal crashes; Tesla's own study cautioned that the comparisons were not causal estimates. Reuters also documented pressure on Dutch regulators, who said their review remained independent. The case highlights the difference between measured proxies and validated safety outcomes.
